blocks.text: One mechanic at a roadside workshop lifts the corner of a lorry with a small jack he turns using one hand. He has not become stronger — the jack simply makes him move his hand a very long way so that the lorry moves a very short way. Every machine trades distance for force.

blocks.markdown:
A **machine** is any device that lets a force applied at one point overcome a resisting force at another point. The force you apply is the **effort**; the force you overcome is the **load**.

Two ratios describe every machine:

$$\text{MA} = \frac{\text{load}}{\text{effort}}, \qquad \text{VR} = \frac{\text{distance moved by effort}}{\text{distance moved by load}}$$

blocks.title: Mechanical advantage and velocity ratio
blocks.text: Mechanical advantage (MA) is the ratio of load to effort — it tells you how many times the machine multiplies your force. Velocity ratio (VR) is the ratio of the distance moved by the effort to the distance moved by the load — it is fixed by the geometry of the machine alone. Both are pure numbers with no unit.

blocks.caption: The key relationship linking the three quantities

blocks.markdown:
Why does that formula work? Efficiency is useful work out over total work in:

$$\eta = \frac{L \times d_L}{E \times d_E} = \frac{L}{E} \times \frac{d_L}{d_E} = \frac{\text{MA}}{\text{VR}}$$

Because efficiency can never exceed 100%, **MA is always less than VR** for a real machine. The velocity ratio depends only on the geometry, so it never changes; MA falls as friction rises.

blocks.title: A block and tackle
blocks.prompt: A block and tackle system with 4 pulleys is used to raise a load of 500 N by applying an effort of 150 N. Calculate (a) the mechanical advantage, (b) the velocity ratio and (c) the efficiency.

steps.text: Mechanical advantage is load divided by effort.
For a block and tackle, the velocity ratio equals the number of pulleys, which is the number of rope sections supporting the load.
Interpret: about 17% of the work done by the effort goes into friction at the pulley axles and into lifting the movable block itself.

blocks.title: An inclined plane
blocks.prompt: A plank 10 m long is used as a ramp to slide a 500 N drum onto a lorry platform 2.0 m high. The effort needed is 125 N. Find the velocity ratio, the mechanical advantage and the efficiency of the ramp.

steps.text: The velocity ratio of an inclined plane is the length of the slope divided by the vertical height.
Mechanical advantage is load over effort.
Check the energy accounts: the effort does 125 × 10 = 1250 J while the drum gains 500 × 2.0 = 1000 J, and 1000 ÷ 1250 = 80%, confirming the result.

blocks.title: A machine never multiplies energy
blocks.text: A jack lets you lift a lorry with one hand, but you must turn the handle through a huge total distance. Force is multiplied; energy is not. The work you put in always exceeds the work the load receives, because friction takes its share.

blocks.title: WAEC and NECO tip
blocks.text: For a pulley question, count the rope sections that actually pull upwards on the movable block — that number is the velocity ratio. Do not count the section you hold if it leaves the fixed block downwards.

points: Mechanical advantage = load ÷ effort; velocity ratio = distance moved by effort ÷ distance moved by load. Both are pure numbers.
Efficiency = MA ÷ VR × 100 %, so MA is always less than VR for a real machine.
Velocity ratio depends only on the geometry of the machine and is unaffected by friction.
For a block and tackle VR equals the number of supporting rope sections; for an inclined plane VR = slope length ÷ height.
Machines multiply force but never energy — the extra distance you move the effort is what pays for it.
